steps.observation: Work on this for 900 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Below is a thorough—but reasonably concise—overview of the principal differences between RNA (ribonucleic acid) and DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid). It touches on chemical structure, physical properties, biological roles, evolutionary context, and practical laboratory considerations.

1. Sugar component  
   • DNA: 2-deoxyribose (lacks a hydroxyl group at the 2ʹ carbon).  
   • RNA: ribose (has a hydroxyl group at the 2ʹ carbon).  
   Consequences: The extra 2ʹ-OH in RNA makes the molecule more chemically reactive and less stable, particularly under alkaline conditions; that same reactivity allows RNA to adopt catalytic (ribozyme) roles.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • Shared: adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C).  
   • DNA-specific: thymine (T).  
   • RNA-specific: uracil (U) in place of thymine.  
   Consequences: Uracil is energetically cheaper to synthesize. DNA uses thymine because 5-methyl-uracil (thymine) helps in repair systems that detect deamination of cytosine to uracil.

3. Strand architecture  
   • DNA: usually double-stranded, forming a right-handed helical duplex (B-form in cells).  
   • RNA: typically single-stranded but can fold into local double-stranded stems and complex 3-D structures (tRNA, rRNA, ribozymes, etc.).  
   Consequences: Double-stranded DNA provides robust long-term information storage; RNA’s structural versatility enables catalytic activity and regulation.

4. Functional specializations  
   DNA  
   – Long-term storage of genetic information.  
   – Template for replication and transcription.  
   – In eukaryotes, largely confined to the nucleus (or organelles such as mitochondria, chloroplasts).  

   RNA  
   – Messenger RNA (mRNA): conveys coding information from DNA to ribosomes.  
   – Ribosomal RNA (rRNA): structural/catalytic core of the ribosome.  
   – Transfer RNA (tRNA): adaptor that matches amino acids to codons.  
   – Non-coding RNAs: microRNA, siRNA, lncRNA, snRNA, snoRNA—gene regulation, splicing, modification, chromatin remodeling.  
   – Catalytic RNAs (ribozymes): e.g., self-splicing introns, RNase P.  

5. Stability and repair  
   • DNA: chemically more stable; cells devote extensive repair machinery (base-excision, nucleotide-excision, mismatch repair, homologous recombination).  
   • RNA: short-lived in many contexts (mRNA half-lives minutes to hours); fewer dedicated repair systems, degradation often regulated for gene-expression control.

6. Location and lifecycle  
   • DNA: mostly nuclear; replicated once per cell cycle.  
   • RNA: synthesized in nucleus (or nucleoid in prokaryotes) and functions throughout cytoplasm; turnover is dynamic.

7. Replication vs. transcription  
   • DNA polymerases require a primer, incorporate dNTPs, possess proofreading exonuclease activity.  
   • RNA polymerases initiate de novo, incorporate NTPs, lower fidelity, no 3ʹ→5ʹ proofreading.

8. Chemical reactivity and enzymatic usage  
   • The 2ʹ-OH of RNA participates in intramolecular transesterification: basis of self-splicing and alkaline lability.  
   • Reverse transcriptase and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase exploit RNA templates; DNA replicases do not.

9. Epigenetic/chemical modifications  
   • DNA: methylation at cytosine (5mC), adenine (6mA in prokaryotes), hydroxymethylcytosine, etc.—key for gene regulation and genome defense.  
   • RNA: extensive modifications (m6A, ψ, m5C, inosine) fine-tune stability, translation, localization.

10. Evolutionary context  
    • RNA World hypothesis: early life may have relied solely on RNA for both information storage and catalysis; DNA and proteins emerged later for improved stability and functional diversity.

11. Practical laboratory distinctions  
    • Stability: RNA easily degraded by ubiquitous RNases; labs need RNase-free reagents and surfaces.  
    • UV absorption: both absorb at 260 nm; OD260 quantitation requires different extinction coefficients.  
    • Manipulations: reverse transcription converts RNA → cDNA for PCR; DNA can be directly amplified.

Key takeaway  
DNA’s deoxyribose backbone and double-helix architecture make it an exceptionally stable repository of genetic information, while RNA’s ribose backbone and versatile single-stranded structures allow it to serve as messenger, scaffold, regulator, and catalyst.
